summary:
This A/B evaluation covered 4 evals in the SageMaker/governance domain, though one ("negative-sagemaker-eval-failed") was fully skipped because it was a should_trigger:false test, so no data is available there for either variant. The other three evals ("training-job-failed-malformed-data", "capacity-vs-quota", "model-registry-approval") produced mixed, non-decisive results across variants, with no quality-comparison pairs evaluated in any eval (all marked pairs_skipped), so output-quality judgments and output-consistency (run-to-run stability) could not be assessed at all for either variant.

Trigger firing was 100% for both variants on all three active evals — this dimension shows no difference.

Expected-output pass rates diverged by eval:
- training-job-failed-malformed-data: with_skill met expected output 1/1, without_skill 0/1 (both at medium confidence).
- capacity-vs-quota: both variants failed expected output (0/1), confidence high — i.e., neither variant met the bar here, suggesting this task or its expectation is hard for both.
- model-registry-approval: both variants failed expected output (0/1) too (medium/high confidence) — again neither succeeded.
So on expected-output, with_skill only "won" the first eval; the other two were failures for both.

Per-assertion results showed real but inconsistent splits:
- training-job-failed-malformed-data: without_skill passed more assertions overall (4/6 vs 3/6). One assertion (distinguishing data-validation vs capacity failure) passed only for without_skill; one (reading status fields) and one (not prescribing fixes for pending jobs) passed for both; two assertions (training check-id citation, LLM-SM check-id presence) failed for both, meaning those behaviors are not yet working for either variant.
- capacity-vs-quota: without_skill passed more assertions (2/6 vs 1/6). Two assertions passed only for without_skill (distinguishing capacity vs quota causes, and correct capacity/quota-specific remediation). One assertion (no raw account ID exposed) passed only for with_skill, with without_skill failing it. Two assertions (reading quota value as evidence, citing check-id+command) failed for both variants.
- model-registry-approval: with_skill passed notably more assertions (4/5 vs 1/5). Three assertions passed only for with_skill: using a command-only remediation (not calling mutating APIs), including an LLM-SM registry check-id, and not exposing raw account IDs — notably without_skill's failure on the command-only assertion was flagged with low confidence, which weakens that specific finding. One assertion (reading approval status) passed for both. One assertion (flagging pending/rejected packages as findings) failed for both.

So directionally, without_skill did better on assertions in the first two evals while with_skill did much better on assertions in the third eval — there isn't a consistent per-dimension leader across tasks.

On runtime and cost, without_skill was consistently faster and cheaper than with_skill across all three active evals: e.g., training-job eval (29s/$0.25 vs 42s/$0.35), capacity-vs-quota (9s/$0.08 vs 1m55s/$0.96 — a large gap), and model-registry (19s/$0.16 vs 26s/$0.22). Context window utilization was also somewhat lower for without_skill throughout, with no compactions for either variant in any eval.

Overall, the picture is mixed rather than a clear pattern: without_skill was faster/cheaper in every active eval, and had more assertion passes in two of three evals, but with_skill had the stronger assertion pass rate and the only expected-output success in one eval (model-registry-approval, and training-job-failed-malformed-data respectively, split across tasks). Several assertions failed for both variants in every eval (e.g., check-id citation/command-style remediation), pointing to a shared gap in behavior rather than a variant-specific issue. No quality or consistency data exists to corroborate these differences, and one eval was not applicable at all, so confidence in any overall characterization is limited.

training-job-failed-malformed-data.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task about diagnosing a SageMaker training job failure. The behavior under test (trigger) fired successfully in the one case tested.

On the top-line "expected output" check, with_skill met the expected outcome (1/1, medium confidence) while without_skill did not (0/1, medium confidence). Since this is based on a single task instance, this is a notable but low-sample-size difference, not a broad pattern.

Looking at the six underlying assertions (also from this single task, so each is a single pass/fail data point, not a rate):
- Two assertions passed for both variants: reading DescribeTrainingJob status/SecondaryStatus/FailureReason instead of guessing, and correctly not prescribing a config/data fix when the job is actually waiting on capacity rather than failed. These don't differentiate the variants.
- Two assertions failed for both variants: citing a specific training sub-family check-id with a safe, non-mutating command recommendation, and including an LLM-SM training check-id via regex. These point to a shared gap in both variants' behavior (or possibly a demanding assertion) rather than a difference between them.
- One assertion diverged: without_skill correctly distinguished a data-validation failure from a capacity failure, while with_skill did not (conflated the two). This is the clearest variant-to-variant difference in the assertion data.
- One "no raw account ID exposed" assertion passed for both, a basic safety check that both variants satisfy.

Net assertion pass rates were 3/6 (50%) for with_skill and 4/6 (67%) for without_skill, driven mainly by the one diverging assertion above plus the overall expected-output mismatch.

On runtime and cost, with_skill took longer (~42s vs ~29s, about 13s more) and cost more (~$0.35 vs ~$0.25) than without_skill. Context window utilization was low for both (7.7% vs 5.4%), with no compaction events for either, indicating neither strained context limits.

Quality-comparison pairs could not be evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 1 skipped), so no direct side-by-side quality judgment is available. Output consistency across repeated runs is also not available for either variant (null), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed here.

Overall, this is a single-task evaluation with limited statistical weight. The data shows without_skill meeting the expected output and correctly distinguishing failure types where with_skill did not, while also running faster and at lower cost. However, both variants shared the same gaps in citing a specific check-id and providing a safe remediation command. With quality-pair and consistency data unavailable, and the sample being a single task, these findings should be read as a limited, single-instance signal rather than a robust comparison.

capacity-vs-quota.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task about diagnosing a SageMaker training issue (distinguishing capacity shortfall vs. zero service quota, citing a check-id, and avoiding exposure of account IDs). The trigger condition for the test did fire (1/1).

Neither variant met the overall expected output (0/1 for both), and this judgment was made with high confidence, so this is a reasonably solid finding that both fell short of the full expected bar, not an artifact of weak measurement.

On the six underlying assertions, without_skill passed 2/6 (33%) and with_skill passed 1/6 (17%) — both low in absolute terms. Breaking this down shows where the real differences (and lack of differences) lie:
- Two assertions failed for both variants (always_fails): reading the service-quota value as evidence rather than assuming the cause, and citing the relevant training check-id with a runnable remediation command. These point to shared gaps in behavior that neither variant handled, rather than a difference between them.
- Two assertions were passed only by without_skill and failed by with_skill: distinguishing capacity-shortfall vs. zero-quota root causes with correct opposite remediations, and prescribing the correct remediation (retry/alternate-instance vs. quota-increase) for each case specifically. These are meaningful, high-confidence distinctions favoring without_skill.
- One assertion was passed only by with_skill and failed by without_skill: not exposing a raw 12-digit account ID. This is a real difference favoring with_skill and matters for the governance/security angle of the task.
- One regex-based assertion ("at least one finding carries an LLM-SM training check-id") failed for both, reinforcing that this specific capability is missing regardless of variant.

On runtime and cost, without_skill was substantially faster (about 9 seconds vs. about 1 minute 55 seconds for with_skill) and cheaper (about $0.08 vs. $0.96), with modestly lower context-window utilization (4.4% vs. 7.3%); neither used context compaction. These are sizeable efficiency differences, but since neither variant achieved the expected output and assertion coverage is partial and mixed, it would be inaccurate to treat the efficiency gap alone as decisive.

No quality-comparison pairs were evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 1 skipped), and output consistency across repeated runs is not available for either variant (null), so neither of those dimensions can inform this summary — they are simply absent data, not evidence of poor or stable performance either way.

Overall, this is a single-task, single-run evaluation with limited assertion coverage: both variants missed the expected output outright, shared two core failure points, but differed on three assertions — two favoring without_skill's causal/remediation reasoning and one favoring with_skill's handling of account-ID exposure — alongside a clear efficiency gap favoring without_skill. Given the small sample size and missing quality/consistency data, these results should be read as suggestive rather than conclusive.

model-registry-approval.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat task testing whether an AWS DevOps agent correctly handles SageMaker model package approval status checks. The trigger behavior under test fired successfully (1/1).

Neither variant met the overall "expected output" criterion (0/1 for both), though the confidence behind that judgment differs: medium confidence for with_skill vs. high confidence for without_skill. Since both failed this top-level check, this dimension does not differentiate them, but it does suggest the core task scenario is one that neither variant handled as the evaluator deemed fully correct.

At the per-assertion level, a more nuanced picture emerges across 5 assertions:
- One assertion (reading ModelApprovalStatus rather than assuming approval) passed for both variants — this is not a differentiator.
- One assertion (flagging a PendingManualApproval/Rejected package being served, and recommending only Approved deployments) failed for both variants — this indicates either the assertion or the underlying agent behavior needs work, since neither variant satisfies it.
- Three assertions differentiated the variants, each passing for with_skill and failing for without_skill: (1) recommending remediation as an operator command rather than calling a mutating API directly (without_skill's failure here was flagged with low confidence, weakening certainty in that specific result), (2) including an LLM-SM registry check-id in findings, and (3) avoiding exposure of a raw 12-digit account ID.

Overall assertion pass rates were 4/5 (80%) for with_skill and 1/5 (20%) for without_skill, driven by the three assertions above.

On runtime and cost, without_skill was faster (~19s vs ~26s) and cheaper (~$0.16 vs ~$0.22), with lower context window utilization (4.8% vs 6.6%); neither variant triggered any context compaction. These efficiency gains for without_skill should be weighed against its lower assertion pass rate.

No quality comparison pairs were evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 1 skipped), so no direct quality-preference signal is available between the variants. Output consistency across repeated runs was not measured for either variant (null for both), so run-to-run stability cannot be assessed here.

In summary: the two variants tie on the overall expected-output metric (both failed, though with different confidence levels) and on one assertion each direction (one shared pass, one shared fail), but with_skill passed three additional assertions that without_skill failed, including one where without_skill's failure was noted as low-confidence. without_skill was notably faster and cheaper. No quality-pairwise or consistency data exists to contextualize these differences further, and the sample size is just one task, so these findings should be treated as a single data point rather than a robust trend.
